tips.title: Three greenhouse gases
tips.body: **water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane**. Water vapour is the one most often forgotten, and it is first on the specification's list. Oxygen and nitrogen are **not** greenhouse gases, which is worth knowing when a question offers them.

tips.title: Short wave in, long wave out
tips.body: The mechanism in six words: **short wavelength in, long wavelength trapped**. Radiation from the Sun arrives at **short** wavelength and passes through; the Earth re-emits at **long** wavelength, and that is what greenhouse gases **absorb**.

tips.title: The greenhouse effect is not the problem
tips.body: Greenhouse gases **maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life**. Without them the planet would be frozen. The concern is the **increase** caused by human activity, not the effect itself — and a question about *the greenhouse effect* usually wants the useful version.

tips.title: Two activities per gas
tips.body: The spec asks you to **recall two human activities that increase each gas**. **Carbon dioxide**: burning fossil fuels and deforestation. **Methane**: cattle farming and rice paddy fields and landfill. Giving one of each is half an answer.

tips.title: A carbon footprint covers the whole life cycle
tips.body: It is the **total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event** — not just the emissions from using it. Making, transporting and disposing of it all count.

why.matters:
The greenhouse effect is not the problem. It is the reason the planet is habitable: without it the surface would average well below freezing. The specification says so in its first line, and a question about *the greenhouse effect* usually wants that.

What this topic is really teaching is how to argue about a system too complicated to model exactly — where the mechanism is certain, the size of the effect is not, and *uncertain* has to be distinguished from *unknown* in your own answer.

examples.title: Why the Earth is not frozen
examples.body:
Sunlight arrives at **short** wavelength and passes straight through the atmosphere. The warmed ground re-emits it at **long** wavelength, and that is the radiation greenhouse gases absorb and send back down in all directions.

Take them away and the surface would average about **-18 °C** instead of **15 °C** — 33 degrees of difference, and the difference between a planet with oceans and one without. The Moon, at the same distance from the Sun with no atmosphere at all, swings from boiling to far below anything on Earth between its day and its night.

visual.alt: A table of surface temperatures: Earth averaging about fifteen degrees Celsius, the same Earth without greenhouse gases at about minus eighteen, and the Moon with no atmosphere swinging from a hundred and twenty by day to minus a hundred and seventy at night

examples.title: The cow and the landfill
examples.body:
Carbon dioxide gets the attention, and methane is the one that surprises people. A cow is a fermentation vessel: the microbes that let it digest grass give off methane, and it belches most of it out.

Landfill does the same thing underground, and a flooded rice field is another airless place where things rot without oxygen. None of that involves a chimney or an exhaust pipe, which is exactly why the specification asks for **two** activities per gas — the obvious one and the one you would not have guessed.

examples.title: A footprint is the whole life, not the tailpipe
examples.body:
A carbon footprint is the total of the greenhouse gases emitted over the **full life** of a product — making it, moving it, using it, and getting rid of it at the end.

That is why the argument about an electric car is about the battery, and why a reusable bag has to be used many times before it beats the one it replaced. Counting only the stage you can see gives an answer that feels right and is not the total, which is the whole reason the definition insists on the word *life*.

steps.title: The greenhouse effect
steps.body:
**Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life.** That sentence comes first in the specification, and it matters: the greenhouse effect is what makes the planet habitable.

**The three greenhouse gases named are water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane.**

**The mechanism**, which the spec asks you to describe in terms of **the interaction of short and long wavelength radiation with matter**:

1. Radiation from the Sun reaches the Earth as **short wavelength** radiation.
2. It **passes through** the atmosphere, because greenhouse gases do not absorb it.
3. It is **absorbed by the Earth's surface**, which **warms up**.
4. The warmed Earth **re-emits** energy, but at a **longer wavelength** — infrared.
5. **Greenhouse gases absorb this long wavelength radiation** and **re-emit it in all directions**, including **back towards the Earth**.
6. So energy is **trapped** in the atmosphere and the Earth stays warm.

**The key idea is the change of wavelength.** The same greenhouse gases that let the incoming radiation straight through **absorb** the outgoing radiation, because it is at a different wavelength. Without that asymmetry there would be no greenhouse effect at all.

**A caution about the word *reflect*.** Greenhouse gases **absorb and re-emit**; they do not simply bounce the radiation back. Mark schemes are strict about this, because *reflect* describes a mirror and misses the mechanism.

**Oxygen and nitrogen are not greenhouse gases**, even though they make up almost all of the atmosphere. Being a greenhouse gas is about **absorbing long wavelength radiation**, not about being abundant.

steps.title: Human activities
steps.body:
**Some human activities increase the amounts of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere**, and the spec asks you to **recall two human activities that increase the amounts of each** of carbon dioxide and methane.

**Carbon dioxide:**

- **burning fossil fuels** — coal, oil and gas contain carbon that was **locked away** over millions of years, and burning them **releases it** as carbon dioxide.
- **deforestation** — fewer trees means **less photosynthesis**, so less carbon dioxide is removed. Burning the cleared timber releases more.

**Methane:**

- **cattle farming** — cattle produce methane as they digest, and herds have grown with demand for meat and dairy.
- **rice paddy fields and landfill** — flooded rice fields and buried waste both decay **without oxygen**, which produces methane.

**Notice that deforestation works the other way round from the rest.** Burning fossil fuels **adds** carbon dioxide; deforestation **removes the thing that was taking it away**. Both raise the amount in the air, but by different routes, and saying which is which is a mark.

**What follows.** **Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe that human activities will cause the temperature of the Earth's atmosphere to increase at the surface**, and that this will result in **global climate change**.

**That sentence is carefully worded and worth copying.** It says *based on peer-reviewed evidence* and *many scientists believe* — not *it is proved*. The specification wants you to represent the science accurately, including its uncertainty.

steps.title: Why the science is hard to be certain about
steps.body:
**It is difficult to model such complex systems as global climate change.** The spec spends a whole section on this, and questions on it are common because they test scientific literacy rather than recall.

**Why modelling is hard:**

- The climate has an enormous number of **interacting variables**.
- Models must be **simplified** to be usable, and simplification introduces **uncertainty**.
- Predictions run **decades or centuries** ahead, so they cannot be checked quickly.

**What that leads to**, in the specification's own words: **simplified models, speculation, and opinions presented in the media that may be based on only parts of the evidence and which may be biased.**

**So a report is not the same as the evidence.** A newspaper article may quote one study, omit the rest, or be written to support a position. Evaluating **the quality of the evidence** means asking:

- Is it based on **peer-reviewed** research?
- Does it use **all** the evidence, or a selected part?
- Who produced it, and might they be **biased**?
- Is a **single** result being presented as a settled conclusion?

**Why peer review matters.** Before publication, other scientists check the methods and the reasoning. It does not make a result certain, but it filters out work that does not stand up — which is why *peer-reviewed* appears in the specification's own sentence about what scientists believe.

**And why communicating results matters.** Findings have to reach the public and policymakers if they are to be acted on. That is also where distortion enters, which is exactly why being able to **describe the uncertainties** honestly is part of the skill.

steps.title: Effects, and the carbon footprint
steps.body:
**An increase in average global temperature is a major cause of climate change**, and the spec asks you to **describe briefly four potential effects**:

1. **sea level rise, causing flooding and coastal erosion**
2. **more frequent and more severe storms**
3. **changes to the amount and distribution of rainfall**
4. **changes to the distribution of species, and loss of habitats**

**You are also asked to discuss the scale, risk and environmental implications.** Those are three different questions: **how big** the effect is, **how likely** it is, and **what it does to the environment**. An answer that treats every effect as certain and catastrophic has not discussed risk.

**The carbon footprint** is **the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event**.

**The words *full life cycle* are the whole idea.** It is not just the emissions when something is used — it includes **obtaining the raw materials, manufacturing, transporting, using and disposing of** it. A product that is clean in use may still have a large footprint if making it was not.

**The carbon footprint can be reduced by reducing emissions of carbon dioxide and methane**, and the spec asks for **actions** and for **reasons why actions may be limited**.

**Actions:**

- using **renewable energy** or nuclear rather than fossil fuels
- improving **energy efficiency**, so less fuel is needed
- **carbon capture and storage**, trapping carbon dioxide before it reaches the air
- **carbon taxes** and **licences**, making emissions cost money
- **carbon offsetting**, such as planting trees
- eating **less meat and dairy**, reducing methane from cattle

**Why actions may be limited:**

- they **cost** a great deal, and some countries cannot afford them
- there may be a **lack of political will**, or **disagreement** between countries
- the **technology** may not yet exist or be reliable at scale
- people are **unwilling to change their lifestyles**
- there is **incomplete education** and **information** about what is needed

**Being able to give the limits is half of this spec point.** A question asking why more is not being done wants these, not a general statement that it is difficult.

steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the three greenhouse gases given in the specification.
2. Give two human activities that increase carbon dioxide.

**Part B.**

4. Describe the greenhouse effect in terms of short and long wavelength radiation.

**Part C.**

8. Explain why it is difficult to be certain about predictions of climate change, and what makes some evidence more reliable than other evidence.
9. Give three actions that would reduce a carbon footprint, and for each give a reason it may be limited.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Absorb and re-emit, never reflect.** Greenhouse gases **absorb** long wavelength radiation and **re-emit it in all directions**, some of it back towards the surface. *Reflect* describes a mirror and misses the mechanism entirely, and mark schemes reject it.

**The wavelength change is the mechanism.** Incoming radiation is **short** wavelength and passes straight through; the Earth re-emits at **long** wavelength, and that is what gets absorbed. If the outgoing radiation were the same wavelength as the incoming, there would be no greenhouse effect. Making that asymmetry explicit is what turns a description into an explanation.

**The greenhouse effect is not the problem.** It **maintains temperatures high enough to support life**. The concern is the **enhanced** effect caused by rising concentrations. An answer that treats the greenhouse effect itself as harmful has misread the specification's first sentence.

**Deforestation works the other way round.** Burning fossil fuels **adds** carbon dioxide; deforestation **removes the process that was taking it away**. Both raise the concentration, by opposite mechanisms, and distinguishing them is a routine mark.

**Evaluating evidence means asking about the source, not just the claim.** Is it **peer reviewed**? Does it use **all** the evidence or a **selected part**? Might the source be **biased**? Is a **single** study being presented as proof? The specification explicitly mentions **speculation and opinions in the media that may be based on only parts of the evidence**, so a question showing you a newspaper report is asking exactly this.

**And uncertainty is not the same as doubt about everything.** Models are **simplified** because the system is **complex**, and predictions run decades ahead. That makes the **scale and timing** uncertain — it does not mean the underlying evidence is weak. A grade 9 answer separates *what is well supported* from *what is hard to predict precisely*.

**Carbon footprint is a whole-life-cycle measure**, and the limits on reducing it are as examinable as the actions. **Cost**, **political disagreement**, **immature technology**, **unwillingness to change lifestyle** and **lack of information** are the specification's territory, and the best answers pair each action with the limit that actually applies to it.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Greenhouse gases maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life.**
- The three named are **water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane**.
- **Short wavelength** radiation from the Sun **passes through** the atmosphere and is **absorbed by the surface**.
- The warmed Earth **re-emits at long wavelength** (infrared).
- **Greenhouse gases absorb the long wavelength radiation** and **re-emit it in all directions**, including back to the surface.
- They **absorb and re-emit**; they do **not reflect**.
- **Carbon dioxide** is increased by **burning fossil fuels** and **deforestation**.
- **Methane** is increased by **cattle farming** and **rice paddy fields and landfill**.
- **Deforestation** raises carbon dioxide by **reducing photosynthesis**, not by releasing it.
- **Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe** human activities will raise surface temperature and cause **global climate change**.
- **Climate change is difficult to model**, so there are **simplified models, speculation and media opinions** that may use **only parts of the evidence** and may be **biased**.
- **Peer review** means other scientists check the methods and reasoning.
- Four potential effects: **sea level rise, causing flooding and coastal erosion**; **more frequent and more severe storms**; **changes to the amount and distribution of rainfall**; **changes to the distribution of species, and loss of habitats**.
- Discuss **scale, risk and environmental implications** — three different questions.
- A **carbon footprint** is the **total greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle** of a product, service or event.
- Reduce it by **renewables, energy efficiency, carbon capture and storage, carbon taxes, offsetting**, and **less meat and dairy**.
- Actions are limited by **cost, political disagreement, immature technology, unwillingness to change lifestyle** and **lack of information**.

questions.prompt: Describe the greenhouse effect in terms of short and long wavelength radiation, and explain how human activities are increasing it.
questions.solution:
**Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life.** Without them the planet would be far colder than it is, so the greenhouse effect itself is not a problem — the concern is the **increase** caused by human activity. The gases named by the specification are **water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane**. Note that **nitrogen and oxygen are not greenhouse gases**, even though they make up almost all of the air: what matters is **absorbing long wavelength radiation**, not being abundant.

The mechanism depends on a **change of wavelength**. Radiation reaches the Earth from the Sun as **short wavelength** radiation. Greenhouse gases do **not** absorb at that wavelength, so it **passes through the atmosphere** and is **absorbed by the Earth's surface**, which **warms up**.

The warmed surface then **re-emits energy**, but at a **longer wavelength** — infrared. **This** is the radiation that **greenhouse gases absorb**. Having absorbed it, they **re-emit it in all directions**, and some of it travels **back towards the surface**. Energy is therefore trapped within the atmosphere rather than escaping directly to space, and the Earth stays warm.

It is worth being precise about two things here. First, the gases **absorb and re-emit** — they do not **reflect**, which describes a mirror and misses the mechanism. Second, the **asymmetry between the two wavelengths is the whole effect**: if the outgoing radiation were the same wavelength as the incoming, it would escape as easily as it arrived.

**Human activities are increasing the amounts of these gases.** Carbon dioxide is increased by **burning fossil fuels**, which releases carbon that was locked away in coal, oil and gas over millions of years, and by **deforestation**. Methane is increased by **cattle farming**, since cattle produce methane as they digest, and by **rice paddy fields and landfill**, where material decays **without oxygen**.

Deforestation is worth distinguishing from the others, because it works the opposite way round. Burning fossil fuels **adds** carbon dioxide to the air; deforestation **removes the process that was taking it away**, since fewer trees means **less photosynthesis**. Both raise the concentration, but by different routes.

**Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe** that these increases will raise the temperature of the Earth's atmosphere at the surface, resulting in **global climate change**.

Note that **nitrogen and oxygen are not greenhouse gases**, even though they make up almost all of the air: what matters is **absorbing long wavelength radiation**, not being abundant.

The mechanism depends on a **change of wavelength**. Radiation reaches the Earth from the Sun as **short wavelength** radiation. Greenhouse gases do **not** absorb at that wavelength, so it **passes through the atmosphere** and is **absorbed by the Earth's surface**, which **warms up**.

The warmed surface then **re-emits energy**, but at a **longer wavelength** — infrared. **This** is the radiation that **greenhouse gases absorb**. Having absorbed it, they **re-emit it in all directions**, and some of it travels **back towards the surface**. Energy is therefore trapped within the atmosphere rather than escaping directly to space, and the Earth stays warm.

It is worth being precise about two things here. First, the gases **absorb and re-emit** — they do not **reflect**, which describes a mirror and misses the mechanism. Second, the **asymmetry between the two wavelengths is the whole effect**: if the outgoing radiation were the same wavelength as the incoming, it would escape as easily as it arrived.

**Human activities are increasing the amounts of these gases.** Carbon dioxide is increased by **burning fossil fuels**, which releases carbon that was locked away in coal, oil and gas over millions of years, and by **deforestation**. Methane is increased by **cattle farming**, since cattle produce methane as they digest, and by **rice paddy fields and landfill**, where material decays **without oxygen**.

Deforestation is worth distinguishing from the others, because it works the opposite way round. Burning fossil fuels **adds** carbon dioxide to the air; deforestation **removes the process that was taking it away**, since fewer trees means **less photosynthesis**. Both raise the concentration, but by different routes.

**Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe** that these increases will raise the temperature of the Earth's atmosphere at the surface, resulting in **global climate change**.

questions.prompt: A company claims its new product is "carbon neutral". Evaluate what evidence you would need to judge this claim, and discuss what actions could genuinely reduce a carbon footprint and what limits them.
questions.solution:
A **carbon footprint** is the **total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event**. So the first thing to establish about a "carbon neutral" claim is **what it covers**. A footprint is not just the emissions when something is **used**: it includes obtaining the **raw materials**, **manufacturing**, **transporting**, using **and disposing of** it. A product that releases nothing in use may still have a large footprint if making it consumed a great deal of fossil-fuel energy — so a claim that quietly measures only the use phase is not measuring a carbon footprint at all.

I would then ask about the **evidence** behind the figure, in much the way the specification suggests for reports on climate change. Has the calculation been **independently checked**, or is it the company's own? Is it based on **peer-reviewed** methodology, so that other scientists have examined the reasoning? Does it use **all** the relevant evidence, or has it been **based on only parts of it** — excluding transport, say, or the disposal of the product at the end of its life? And who produced it: the company has a clear interest in the answer, so there is an obvious possibility of **bias**. None of that makes the claim false, but a claim that cannot answer those questions should not be accepted.

I would also ask **how** neutrality is achieved. If it rests on **carbon offsetting** — planting trees, for example — then the emissions are still being **released**; they are being **compensated for** elsewhere, and trees take **decades** to absorb what was emitted immediately. That is a materially weaker claim than one based on **not emitting in the first place**.

Actions that genuinely reduce a footprint include switching to **renewable energy** instead of fossil fuels, improving **energy efficiency** so that less fuel is needed for the same job, and **carbon capture and storage**, which traps carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere. **Carbon taxes and licences** work indirectly, by making emissions cost money, and reducing **meat and dairy** consumption cuts the methane produced by cattle.

Each of these is limited in practice, and the specification asks for those limits as well as the actions. Renewables and carbon capture are **expensive** to build, and some countries **cannot afford** them. Carbon taxes require **political agreement**, often between countries whose interests differ. Carbon capture technology is still **developing** and not yet proven at the scale required. And changes such as eating less meat or flying less depend on people being **willing to change their lifestyles**, which they often are not, partly because of **incomplete information** about what would actually make a difference.

On balance, I would judge such a claim only if it were **independently verified**, covered the **whole life cycle**, and made clear how much of the neutrality came from **reducing emissions** rather than from **offsetting** them.

criteria.text: Defines a carbon footprint as total greenhouse gases over the full life cycle, and states that the claim must cover manufacture, transport, use and disposal.
Questions the evidence: whether it is independently checked or peer reviewed, whether all the evidence is used, and whether the source may be biased.
Gives genuine actions to reduce emissions, such as renewable energy, energy efficiency or carbon capture and storage.
Gives limits on those actions, such as cost, political agreement, immature technology or unwillingness to change lifestyle.

examTechnique.body:
The mechanism question is worth doing precisely: **short wavelength in, absorbed at the surface, re-emitted long, absorbed by greenhouse gases, re-emitted in all directions**. Use **absorb**, never **reflect**, and make the **change of wavelength** explicit.

The rest of the topic is about **evidence and judgement**. When a question says **evaluate** or **discuss**, give both sides and then **decide** — and when it asks about actions, pair each one with the thing that **limits** it.
examinerErrors: Saying greenhouse gases **reflect** radiation instead of **absorbing and re-emitting** it.
Omitting the **change of wavelength**, which is the mechanism.
Treating the greenhouse effect as harmful in itself, when it **keeps the Earth warm enough for life**.
Saying deforestation **releases** carbon dioxide, rather than **reducing photosynthesis**.
Giving only **one** human activity per gas when the spec asks for **two**.
Listing effects without discussing **scale, risk and environmental implications**.
Defining a carbon footprint as the emissions **in use**, rather than over the **full life cycle**.
Giving actions to reduce emissions without the **reasons they may be limited**.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer makes the **wavelength asymmetry** the centre of the mechanism, and explains that without it energy would escape as easily as it arrived. It distinguishes **deforestation** from **combustion** by the route each takes. On evidence it asks about the **source** rather than the claim — peer review, completeness, possible bias — and separates what is **well supported** from what is **hard to predict precisely**, rather than treating uncertainty as doubt about everything. On the carbon footprint it applies the **full life cycle** test to a real claim, notices when **offsetting** is doing the work, and pairs every action with the **limit** that actually applies to it.
